redFlags: Haemodynamic instability, shock, ongoing myocardial ischaemia or severe pulmonary oedema
New focal neurological deficit suggesting stroke
Syncope with a very rapid or very slow ventricular response
Acute decompensated heart failure or pre-excited atrial fibrillation
symptoms: Palpitations or an irregular heartbeat
Breathlessness or reduced exercise tolerance
Fatigue, dizziness, presyncope or syncope
Chest discomfort or presentation with stroke or transient ischaemic attack
physicalSigns: Irregularly irregular pulse
Variable first heart sound and pulse deficit
Tachycardia or, with conduction disease or medication, bradycardia
Signs of heart failure, valve disease or systemic embolism

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Organised flutter activity on electrocardiogram, often with a regular or patterned ventricular response.
Discrete premature P waves with intervening sinus rhythm rather than sustained fibrillatory activity.
At least three P-wave morphologies and an isoelectric baseline, often in severe pulmonary disease.
Consistent P waves and a physiological trigger; careful lead review separates artefact from atrial activity.

ruleIn.testName: 12-lead electrocardiogram
ruleIn.modalityTarget: 12-lead electrocardiogram — Atrial fibrillation
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Irregularly irregular R-R intervals with no consistent discrete P waves.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Provides rhythm confirmation and identifies conduction, ischaemic or pre-excitation features that alter management.

ruleIn.testName: Ambulatory electrocardiographic monitoring
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Ambulatory electrocardiographic monitoring — Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Intermittent electrocardiographically documented atrial fibrillation during symptoms or silent episodes.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Monitoring duration should match symptom frequency when the resting electrocardiogram is normal.

ruleIn.testName: Transthoracic echocardiography when indicated
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Transthoracic echocardiography when indicated — Structural or functional heart disease
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Atrial enlargement, ventricular dysfunction, valve disease or another finding that changes management.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Supports rhythm-control planning, heart-failure assessment and selected refinement of thromboembolic risk.

ruleOut.testName: Thyroid function testing
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Thyroid function testing — Thyrotoxicosis
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No biochemical hyperthyroidism, or a reversible driver is identified.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Thyroid disease can precipitate atrial fibrillation and requires concurrent treatment.

ruleOut.testName: Electrolytes, renal and liver function
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Electrolytes, renal and liver function — Metabolic precipitant or medicine contraindication
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No correctable electrolyte disturbance; organ function is adequate for the selected medicine or prompts adjustment.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Identifies reversible contributors and is essential before anticoagulant or antiarrhythmic selection.

ruleOut.testName: Acute coronary and pulmonary assessment when clinically indicated
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Acute coronary and pulmonary assessment when clinically indicated — Acute coronary syndrome or pulmonary embolism
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No acute ischaemic or thromboembolic trigger, or one is identified and treated through its urgent pathway.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Acute coronary syndrome or pulmonary embolism
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: New atrial fibrillation may be secondary to another time-critical condition.

pathophysiology.summary: Atrial fibrillation is a supraventricular tachyarrhythmia with disorganised atrial activation and ineffective atrial contraction. Irregular ventricular conduction can cause symptoms or tachycardia-mediated dysfunction, while atrial blood stasis promotes thrombus formation and systemic embolism.
keyMechanisms: Ectopic atrial triggers and a susceptible atrial substrate sustain chaotic electrical activation.
Loss of coordinated atrial contraction and irregular atrioventricular conduction reduce haemodynamic efficiency.
Blood stasis, endothelial dysfunction and prothrombotic factors increase left-atrial thrombus and stroke risk.
Hypertension, heart failure, valve disease, thyroid disease, obesity, sleep apnoea and alcohol can promote onset or recurrence.

clinicalManagement.title: Assess stability and reversible triggers
actions: Assess airway, breathing, circulation, ischaemia, heart failure and neurological status.
Obtain a 12-lead electrocardiogram and correct hypoxia, electrolyte disturbance or another precipitant.
Seek senior cardiology/critical-care support for unstable or pre-excited atrial fibrillation.
Perform urgent synchronised electrical cardioversion under the locally approved resuscitation and sedation protocol.
Do not delay emergency cardioversion solely to complete routine anticoagulation assessment.
branches.condition: Life-threatening haemodynamic instability attributable to atrial fibrillation

actions: Proceed to symptom, duration, rate/rhythm and thromboembolic-risk assessment.
branches.condition: No life-threatening instability

clinicalManagement.timeframe: Immediately at acute presentation

clinicalManagement.title: Assess stroke and bleeding risks
actions: Use CHA2DS2-VASc for stroke risk and a validated bleeding-risk tool such as ORBIT.
Identify and modify reversible bleeding risks rather than using a bleeding score alone to withhold anticoagulation.
Discuss absolute benefits, bleeding harms and patient preferences using shared decision making.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: At diagnosis and whenever risk factors change

clinicalManagement.title: Prevent thromboembolism
actions: Offer an SFDA-authorised generic direct-acting oral anticoagulant, such as dabigatran etexilate or rivaroxaban, when indicated and suitable; select using renal function, interactions, adherence and the local formulary.
Use warfarin when a direct-acting anticoagulant is contraindicated, unsuitable, or the clinical condition specifically requires a vitamin-K antagonist.
Do not use antiplatelet monotherapy solely for atrial-fibrillation stroke prevention.
Use current SFDA labelling and the local formulary for all dosing; this record is not a prescribing source.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Promptly after risk assessment

clinicalManagement.title: Choose rate or rhythm control
actions: Use rate control first for many stable patients, with a generic beta-blocker or rate-limiting calcium-channel blocker selected for comorbidity and contraindications.
Consider rhythm control for persistent symptoms, a reversible cause, new onset, atrial flutter suitable for ablation or heart failure thought to be driven by the arrhythmia.
Avoid a rate-limiting calcium-channel blocker in acute decompensated heart failure and obtain specialist advice.
Assess anticoagulation requirements around cardioversion according to rhythm duration and the current protocol.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: During initial management and at symptom review

clinicalManagement.title: Escalate persistent or complex disease
actions: Refer for cardiology review when symptoms remain uncontrolled, recurrence follows cardioversion or antiarrhythmic/ablation decisions are needed.
Consider catheter ablation through specialist shared decision making for eligible symptomatic patients.
Reassess stroke prevention after rhythm restoration because apparent sinus rhythm does not automatically remove thromboembolic risk.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Promptly when initial treatment fails or complexity is identified

nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review symptoms, pulse/rate, blood pressure, anticoagulant adherence, bleeding risk and renal function at a medicine-appropriate interval; reassess stroke risk at least annually and whenever age or comorbidity changes.
mdtReferrals: Cardiology or electrophysiology for rhythm-control and ablation decisions
Anticoagulation or clinical pharmacy service for medicine selection, interactions and adherence
Stroke service for any acute or previous cerebrovascular event
Sleep medicine and weight-management services where relevant
lifestyleAndDiet: Support weight management, regular physical activity and control of blood pressure and diabetes.
Screen for and treat obstructive sleep apnoea when suspected.
Reduce excessive alcohol and stimulant exposure and stop smoking.
For warfarin, advise consistency rather than avoidance of vitamin-K-containing foods and arrange INR education.
patientEducation: Explain the irregular rhythm, symptom-control options and the distinct purpose of anticoagulation.
Teach stroke warning signs and the need for immediate emergency assessment.
Provide medicine-specific bleeding, missed-dose, procedure and interaction advice using approved Saudi information.
dischargeCriteria: Haemodynamics are stable and acute triggers have been addressed.
A rate/rhythm strategy and anticoagulation decision are documented with renal-function-appropriate prescribing.
The patient understands stroke and bleeding precautions and has timely follow-up.

content.title: Breast Cancer Management
content.specialty: Medical Oncology, Breast Surgery and Radiation Oncology

redFlags: Rapidly progressive inflammatory breast change
Spinal pain with weakness, sensory change or bladder/bowel dysfunction
New focal neurological deficit, seizure or raised intracranial-pressure symptoms
Visceral crisis with organ dysfunction requiring rapid oncology assessment
symptoms: New breast or axillary lump
Nipple retraction or bloody discharge
Persistent focal breast change or skin dimpling
Bone pain, breathlessness, neurological symptoms or weight loss in advanced disease
physicalSigns: Discrete breast mass or asymmetric thickening
Peau d'orange, ulceration or inflammatory change
Nipple inversion or eczematous nipple lesion
Palpable axillary or supraclavicular nodes

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Often mobile, well-circumscribed and benign on age-appropriate imaging, but tissue diagnosis is required when assessment is discordant.
Fluid-filled lesion on ultrasound with resolution after aspiration in selected cases.
Pain, erythema, fever and a collection; non-resolution requires investigation for inflammatory malignancy.
History of trauma or surgery with characteristic imaging, although biopsy may be needed if suspicious.

ruleIn.testName: Triple assessment
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Triple assessment — Breast malignancy
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Concordant suspicious clinical examination, mammography/ultrasound and core-biopsy histology.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Integrates anatomy and tissue diagnosis while minimising false reassurance from any single test.

ruleIn.testName: Histopathology with ER, PR and HER2 testing
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Histopathology with ER, PR and HER2 testing — Invasive breast-cancer subtype
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Malignant morphology with grade and validated receptor status.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Confirms diagnosis and directs endocrine, anti-HER2 and chemotherapy decisions.

ruleIn.testName: Stage-directed imaging
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Stage-directed imaging — Regional or distant metastatic disease
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Imaging defines tumour, nodal and metastatic burden when stage or symptoms justify it.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Avoids indiscriminate staging in low-risk disease while identifying treatment-changing metastases.

ruleOut.testName: Image-guided core biopsy of a suspicious benign-appearing lesion
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Image-guided core biopsy of a suspicious benign-appearing lesion — Benign breast disease
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Pathology is benign and concordant with clinical and imaging findings.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Discordance requires repeat sampling or excision rather than simple reassurance.

ruleOut.testName: Targeted imaging of new symptoms
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Targeted imaging of new symptoms — Metastatic complication
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No metastasis explaining the symptom, or a lesion is identified for urgent management.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Routine surveillance imaging in asymptomatic early-stage survivors is not a substitute for symptom-led assessment.

pathophysiology.summary: Breast cancer comprises malignant epithelial tumours with heterogeneous hormone-receptor, HER2 and genomic biology. Disease may remain in situ, invade breast and regional lymphatics, or spread haematogenously to bone, liver, lung and brain; biology and stage jointly determine treatment and prognosis.
keyMechanisms: Accumulated genomic and epigenetic alterations enable uncontrolled proliferation and invasion.
Oestrogen/progesterone-receptor signalling and HER2 amplification define actionable biological subsets.
Lymphatic spread commonly involves axillary and regional nodes.
Tumour heterogeneity and treatment selection pressure can change receptor status in recurrent disease.

clinicalManagement.title: Confirm pathology and stage
actions: Obtain adequate core tissue and report histological type, grade and ER, PR and HER2 status.
Complete stage-appropriate imaging and assess performance status, comorbidities and baseline organ function.
Arrange genetic and fertility counselling when clinical criteria are met.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Before definitive treatment

clinicalManagement.title: Agree a multidisciplinary plan
actions: Discuss every new case in a breast multidisciplinary conference.
Integrate stage, biology, patient goals, surgical feasibility and treatment toxicities.
Record sequence of surgery, systemic therapy and radiotherapy with responsible teams.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: After diagnostic work-up

clinicalManagement.title: Deliver local-regional therapy
actions: Offer breast-conserving surgery or mastectomy according to disease extent, contraindications and informed preference.
Stage the axilla using the appropriate sentinel-node or nodal procedure.
Plan radiotherapy according to surgical approach, margins, nodal involvement and recurrence risk.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: According to stage and treatment sequence

clinicalManagement.title: Select biology-directed systemic therapy
actions: Use endocrine therapy for hormone-receptor-positive disease when indicated.
Use generic anti-HER2 therapy for eligible HER2-positive disease with cardiac monitoring.
Select chemotherapy and any contemporary targeted or immunotherapy only through the current approved oncology protocol.
Prioritise neoadjuvant systemic therapy and serial response assessment.
Proceed to local therapy if disease becomes operable and the MDT confirms benefit.
branches.condition: Locally advanced or inflammatory disease

clinicalManagement.timeframe: Neoadjuvant or adjuvant as agreed by MDT

clinicalManagement.title: Survivorship or advanced-disease review
actions: Use interval history, examination and mammography of retained breast tissue according to policy.
Manage endocrine, bone, cardiac, menopausal and lymphoedema effects.
For metastatic disease, prioritise symptom control, quality of life and biology-directed therapy with early supportive care.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: After initial treatment and throughout follow-up

nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Follow the current Saudi oncology surveillance schedule, including clinical review and mammography where breast tissue remains; monitor therapy-specific cardiac, bone, gynaecological and lymphoedema risks and investigate new symptoms promptly.
mdtReferrals: Breast surgeon, medical oncologist, radiation oncologist and breast-care nurse
Genetics for hereditary-risk criteria
Fertility service before gonadotoxic treatment when relevant
Physiotherapy/lymphoedema, psycho-oncology and palliative care according to need
lifestyleAndDiet: Support regular physical activity and maintenance of a healthy body composition during and after treatment.
Provide dietetic advice for treatment-related weight change, nausea or malnutrition.
Offer smoking-cessation support and advise avoidance of unreviewed supplements that may interact with therapy.
patientEducation: Explain stage, receptor status, treatment intent and the role of each modality in plain language.
Discuss expected adverse effects, fertility, sexual health, pregnancy considerations and when to seek urgent care.
Provide individualised information on recurrence symptoms without encouraging harmful routine self-testing.
dischargeCriteria: The diagnosis, stage, receptor profile and MDT plan are documented.
Acute treatment complications are controlled and the patient has clear contacts.
Surveillance ownership, medicine monitoring and urgent symptom pathways are explicit.

Assess the red flags above and use the current local escalation pathway if instability or rapid deterioration is present.
Explain uncertainty and involve the patient or appropriate decision-maker in a way suited to the setting.
Escalate immediately to the responsible senior or emergency team using the local pathway.
Stabilise and investigate in parallel; do not delay time-critical action for routine testing.
branches.condition: A red flag, instability, or rapid deterioration is present

actions: Proceed with focused assessment and shared planning.
Document the threshold for urgent reassessment.
branches.condition: The person is stable for a planned or longitudinal pathway

clinicalManagement.timeframe: At first contact and whenever the situation changes

clinicalManagement.title: Confirm the working diagnosis and stratify risk
actions: Use the history, examination, and investigations listed above to confirm the likely process and assess important alternatives.
Interpret results using current national/local diagnostic criteria, age, pregnancy status, comorbidity, and prior results.
Record severity, uncertainty, and which findings would change the plan.
Reassess the history and examination and seek senior or specialty advice.
Use targeted additional testing only when its result can change management.
branches.condition: The diagnosis remains uncertain or tests conflict with the clinical picture

actions: Switch to the relevant urgent or specialty pathway.
Communicate the finding and handover responsibility clearly.
branches.condition: A high-risk complication or an alternative diagnosis is identified

clinicalManagement.timeframe: Promptly; adapt timing to acuity

clinicalManagement.title: Agree evidence-informed care and address the cause
actions: Use the topic-specific focus in this record to agree immediate and longer-term priorities with the patient.
Select treatment only after checking current local guidance, formulary, contraindications, interactions, organ function, pregnancy considerations, and patient preference.
Treat reversible contributors and address access, communication, cultural, and functional barriers.
Reassess diagnosis, treatment burden, adherence barriers, and alternatives with the responsible specialist.
Document the shared decision and safety-net plan.
branches.condition: Treatment is ineffective, poorly tolerated, or inconsistent with the patient’s goals

actions: Continue the plan with monitoring proportional to risk.
Provide clear instructions for expected course and warning symptoms.
branches.condition: The patient improves on the agreed plan

clinicalManagement.timeframe: According to acuity and current local protocol

clinicalManagement.title: Coordinate handover, education, and follow-up
actions: Provide a written plan stating the working diagnosis, key findings, medicines or interventions, monitoring, and who owns each next step.
Use teach-back to check that the patient or caregiver understands warning symptoms, follow-up, and how to obtain help.
Close the loop on pending results, referrals, and screening or prevention actions.
Arrange a higher level of care or supported transfer and send a structured clinical handover.
Confirm transport, caregiver, and communication needs where relevant.
branches.condition: Safe care cannot be delivered in the current setting

actions: Confirm a feasible follow-up date and contact route.
Document when and how the plan should be reviewed or escalated.
branches.condition: The patient is ready for outpatient or continuing care

clinicalManagement.timeframe: Before transition and at the agreed review interval

nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review the topic-specific focus, patient goals, symptoms and function at an interval matched to risk. Reconcile new results and treatment effects, close referrals, and revisit the plan if the condition, circumstances, or preferences change.
mdtReferrals: Primary Care / Gynaecology
Primary care or the responsible continuity team
Pharmacist, nurse educator, dietitian, rehabilitation, mental-health, or social support when relevant to the case.
lifestyleAndDiet: Offer topic-relevant prevention or self-management support that is safe, feasible, culturally appropriate, and consistent with the person’s goals.
Avoid one-size-fits-all restrictions; individualise advice for pregnancy, frailty, kidney/heart disease, disability, and treatment burden.
patientEducation: Explain cervical cancer screening and follow-up in plain language, including what is known, what remains uncertain, and how the plan will be reviewed.
Use teach-back for warning signs, medicines or monitoring, and the route to urgent help.
Invite questions and adapt written or interpreted information to the patient’s language, health literacy, and communication needs.
dischargeCriteria: Clinical status is appropriate for the next setting, and urgent complications have been excluded or addressed.
The patient or caregiver has an understandable plan, access to needed treatment/support, and a clear escalation route.
Pending investigations and referrals have a named owner and follow-up timeframe.

redFlags: Possible anaphylaxis after a prior dose
Severe acute illness requiring timing assessment
Immunocompromise or complex vaccine history
Exposure requiring time-sensitive prophylaxis
symptoms: Evaluate the characteristic symptom pattern of Childhood Immunisation and Catch-Up, including onset, evolution, severity, associated symptoms, precipitating factors, complications, and relevant negative findings.
Clarify onset, progression, associated symptoms, baseline function, medicines and the patient’s own priorities.
Ask about relevant risk factors and context described in the case; document important negative findings rather than assuming their absence.
physicalSigns: Record observations and a focused examination directed to the organ system and competing diagnoses in this topic.
Assess functional change, comorbidity, hydration/perfusion where relevant, and baseline status.
Use serial reassessment when the condition or treatment can change over hours or days.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Use registry and prior-provider records; do not assume an undocumented dose was given.
Distinguish severe allergy or live-vaccine restriction from minor illness or expected reaction.
Assess timing and severity; report through local safety pathway.

ruleIn.testName: Review official national registry, written record and prior products/dates; assess age, risk, immune status and allergy history.
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Review official national registry, written record and prior products/dates; assess age, risk, immune status and allergy history. — Childhood Immunisation and Catch-Up
ruleIn.expectedFinding: A result that supports the working diagnosis or defines its severity, interpreted with the clinical picture and current criteria.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Choose this investigation because it can confirm the suspected process, establish baseline risk, or change the next decision in this case.

ruleIn.testName: Use current Saudi MOH/PH authority schedule for catch-up decisions; document product, batch, site and next due date.
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Use current Saudi MOH/PH authority schedule for catch-up decisions; document product, batch, site and next due date. — Cause, complication, or risk relevant to Childhood Immunisation and Catch-Up
ruleIn.expectedFinding: A result that may identify a precipitating factor or complication; interpret in context rather than as a stand-alone diagnosis.
ruleIn.targetCondition: Cause, complication, or risk relevant to Childhood Immunisation and Catch-Up
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: This helps detect an important alternative or complication and informs safe monitoring and referral.

ruleOut.testName: Focused evaluation for the leading alternative diagnoses
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Focused evaluation for the leading alternative diagnoses — Important alternative to Childhood Immunisation and Catch-Up
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Findings that lower the likelihood of the selected alternative; a normal result does not exclude every urgent cause.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Important alternative to Childhood Immunisation and Catch-Up
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: The differential matters because it changes urgency or treatment and should be actively considered.

ruleOut.testName: Serial clinical reassessment with targeted repeat testing when indicated
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Serial clinical reassessment with targeted repeat testing when indicated — Progression or evolving complication
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Stable or improving clinical trend without new evidence of the suspected complication.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: A single early assessment may miss an evolving problem; repeat only when it can guide care.

pathophysiology.summary: Vaccination primes adaptive immune memory and reduces individual disease risk and transmission. Schedule timing, product, immune status, prior doses, and local epidemiology affect protection and catch-up planning. This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.
keyMechanisms: Vaccination primes adaptive immune memory and reduces individual disease risk and transmission. Schedule timing, product, immune status, prior doses, and local epidemiology affect protection and catch-up planning.
Clinical expression and progression vary with baseline risk, comorbidity, treatment exposure, and access to timely care.
